title: A Inventory for the Radiators
premise: August Voss has spent eleven years writing postcards to Lena, whose boarding house burned the night she disappeared, mailing them to a dead address as penance for the lie he told that saved his own skin. When he hears her unfinished song played on the radio—recorded by a stranger who claims to have found her notebook—he learns Lena survived and has been dying slowly in the coastal town they fled. August must return to Graywater Bay, confess the truth of what he did to the man who loved her first, and choose between the loyalty that kept him silent and the truth that might let her forgive him before her time runs out. He arrives too late for reconciliation but in time to sing her song back to her at last; he stays on afterward, keeping the inventory no longer of things unsaid but of everything finally spoken.
about_author: Oscar Pemberton is the pen name of a former archivist who spent two decades cataloguing undelivered letters in a municipal records office. He writes quietly devastating fiction about ordinary people haunted by small betrayals.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: August's POV. We meet him in his meticulous routine: composing postcards to Lena at 14 Alder Lane, filing them by year in an inventory ledger of unsaid things. A neighbor asks why he never moves. The emotional beat is tender compulsion—the reader senses ritual masking guilt without yet knowing why.

chapters.title: A Song Without a Recording
chapters.summary: August's POV. In a café, the radio plays 'The Radiators' Waltz'—a song only Lena ever wrote, hummed once, never recorded. August drops his cup. The radio credits a collector in Graywater Bay. The beat is vertigo: his sealed past cracking open in public.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, August's POV. Eleven years earlier: the night of the fire, the argument with Tomas over Lena, and the lie August told the investigators—that he saw Lena leave alone—to protect himself and damn Tomas's account. The beat is dread; we now understand the inventory's true purpose.

chapters.title: The Collector of Graywater Bay
chapters.summary: August's POV, traveling. He finds Edith Marlowe, the retired music teacher who bought Lena's salvaged notebook from a junk stall. Edith reveals Lena is alive, ill, living above the old cannery—and that she asks visitors one question: 'Did August ever say it?' The beat is hope sharpened into obligation.

chapters.title: Tomas at the Harbor
chapters.summary: August's POV. He seeks Tomas, who stayed in Graywater Bay all these years, believing August's lie. Tomas's bitterness is quiet and total; he warns August that truth arriving this late is just another form of theft. The beat is confrontation without resolution—loyalty and truth pulling opposite ways.

chapters.title: Above the Cannery
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: Lena's voice enters, sharp and unsentimental, describing her illness and her refusal of pity. She watches August from her window before he knocks. The beat is suspended recognition—two people who rehearsed this meeting for a decade, both refusing to perform it.

chapters.title: The Inventory Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. August finally visits and, instead of explaining, reads entries from his ledger aloud—eleven years of postcards never sent to a real address. Lena listens without mercy, correcting his memory where it flattered him. The beat is excruciating intimacy; love re-entering through honesty's side door.

chapters.title: What August Said to the Investigators
chapters.summary: August's POV. He confesses the full lie to Lena and then to Tomas publicly, at the harbor memorial for the fire's other victims. Tomas walks away; some truths repair nothing. The beat is climax: August surrenders his invisibility entirely, accepting whatever verdict follows.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, weakening. Bedridden, she asks August to finish the song's unwritten final verse—not forgiveness, just collaboration. They work on it across three afternoons, arguing about a single chord like they're young again. The beat is grace earned rather than granted.

chapters.title: Everything Finally Spoken
chapters.summary: August's POV, then a coda in Edith's. Lena dies on a morning of gulls and low tide; August sings the finished song at her window. He remains in Graywater Bay, opens a new ledger titled 'Spoken,' and mails one last postcard—to himself, at a live address. The beat is grief transmuted into presence.
